name: Wild Blue Yonder
lede: Wild Blue Yonder is a pale, greyish periwinkle from Wikipedia's color lists, named after the open sky of the phrase "into the wild blue yonder," and distinct from Crayola's darker crayon of the same name.

sections.title: The sky, twice named
sections.body:
This color, #A2ADD0, appears on Wikipedia under "Air Force blue," grouped with the pale, hazy blues associated with flight [1]. "The wild blue yonder" is the opening phrase of the 1939 United States Army Air Corps song, later adopted as the United States Air Force song, where it means the open, limitless sky a pilot flies into [1].

Crayola makes its own crayon called Wild Blue Yonder, a brighter, more saturated blue at #7A89B8, added in 2003 to replace a retired color called Blizzard Blue [3]. The two swatches share a name and a theme but are not the same color [1][3]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pale-greyish-violet-blue]], [[chicory-blue]], [[blue-bell]] and [[pale-soft-blue-violet]], at 2.6, 5.1, 5.2 and 5.4 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this blue in 102 of 23,781 paintings, 0.43 percent, more common than 53 percent of our named colors, as photographed [4]. It plays a hidden color, tucked into shadow rather than light, in 42 percent of its appearances [4]. John Singer Sargent paints it most often among catalogued artists, in 4 of his 287 works here [4]. The earliest dated example is a 1494 panel by Pietro Perugino; print use of the phrase itself only took off after the 1940s, following the song, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4].
